earlier_scan.note: Peripatetic speech register in Afghanistan; Glottolog shows no grammar/phonology; essentially undescribed.

sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 1986. Magati: some notes on an unknown language of northern Afghanistan. JASO: Journal of the Anthropological Society of Oxford 17(2): 135-139.
sources.note: Nothing. p.136: data 'transcribed.. according to the rules of Polish orthography'; p.137: c.30 words and 13 sentences (Man bozor mikinam 'I am going to the bazaar' etc.); p.138: 'the grammatical system was very similar to that of a Persian dialect, whereas the vocabulary seemed to be of mixed origin'; Chistonegi parallels. No accent marks, no prosodic remark.
sources.venue: JASO: Journal of the Anthropological Society of Oxford

sources.citation: Oranskaja, T. I., Ju. V. Mazurova, A. A. Kibrik, L. I. Kulikov & A. Ju. Rusakov (eds.). 2011. Jazyki mira: Novye indoarijskie jazyki [Languages of the World: New Indo-Aryan languages]. Moskva: Academia. 896 pp. ISBN 978-5-87444-394-8.
sources.note: Nothing for Afghan Gorbati: index entry only. The Domari article 2.1.2 gives a stress rule for Jerusalem Domari (morphologically determined, stem-final / on Layer-I and person affixes) and 2.7.0 says other dialects cannot be characterised; volume intro says the small Indo-Aryan idioms of Afghanistan are outside its scope.

sources.citation: Kieffer, Charles M. 1983. AFGHANISTAN v. Languages. Encyclopaedia Iranica I/5: 501-516; and Kieffer 1986 (cited by Pstrusińska 2013:3 n., p.103, listing 'qazūlagī or magadī, or ġorbatī').
sources.note: Kieffer is the Afghan-Persian phonetician of record; his classification note on the Jat argots might characterise them phonologically as Dari.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en): 'Peripatetic groups of Afghanistan', 'Ghorbati people', 'Persian Kowli' (read via API 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. State Ġorbat speak local Persian plus Ghorbati/Magadi/Qāzulāgi, 'a secret language with a heavy Persian base' (citing Rao 1995 pp.74, 85-6; Pstrusińska 2013 p.43).

sources.citation: Pstrusińska, Jadwiga. 2013. Secret Languages of Afghanistan and Their Speakers. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing. ISBN 978-1-4438-4970-8. (30-page publisher sample: front matter, Introduction pp.1-16, start of ch.1)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p.3 n.: Kieffer 1986:103 lists 'qazūlagī or magadī, or ġorbatī' among Jat secret languages. p.14: 'Apart from a few cases, we know little about the real phonetic realization of Middle Asian or Afghan argotic vocabulary.. it would be of little value to attempt to introduce more precise phonological features into the argotic lexical material listed in the present work.' i.e. the fullest modern survey is explicitly lexical, no prosody. Chapter Four (pp.36-87, not in sample) covers the individual argots.

sources.citation: Hanifi, M. Jamil. 2008. JĀT. Encyclopaedia Iranica (online edition). doi:10.1163/2330-4804_EIRO_COM_3956
sources.note: Only: 'Their language is generally called Ḡorbati, Magadi in Herat, and Quzulagi in Kabul and Kandahar.' No linguistic description; pointer value only (bibliography: Olesen 1994 Afghan Craftsmen; Olesen 2000; Rao 1982 Eastern Anthropologist 35(2):115-34).

sources.citation: Windfuhr, Gernot L. 2002 (last updated 2012). GYPSY ii. Gypsy Dialects. Encyclopaedia Iranica XI/4: 415-421.
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Lists 'Persian-based Gypsy groups of Afghanistan: Ḡorbat, endonym, widely found, language also named Qāzulāgi in Herat, Magadi in Kabul region.. (Rao, 1995)' and states 'Most other dialects and variants of Gypsy in these regions are based on local variants of Persian, having adopted both morphology and syntax'; gives one Ḡorbati-of-Afghanistan sentence example from Rao 1995. Second-hand (cites Rao 1995).

Rao, Aparna. 1995. Marginality and language use: the example of peripatetics in Afghanistan. Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society (5th ser.) 5(2): 69-95.
sources.note: Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description source and the primary source behind Windfuhr's Iranica entry; the only publication with first-hand Ġorbati sentence material (pp.74, 85-86); if any remark on pronunciation/prosody of the argot exists it is here.
sources.venue: Journal of the Gypsy Lore Society (5th ser.)

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1994. Peripatetics of Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey. In John Middleton & Amal Rassam (eds.), Encyclopedia of World Cultures, vol. IX: Africa and the Middle East, 274-276. Boston: G. K. Hall. (Glottolog ref 326078; read in the encyclopedia.com reprint.)
sources.note: 'Adurgari (spoken by the Sheikh Mohammadi), Mogatibey (spoken by the Jogi), or Qazulagi, spoken by the Ghorbat — have affinities with languages spoken by similar communities in parts of Iran and also in parts of Central Asia. Their vocabularies also contain Arabic words, but a large percentage of words are of an as yet unknown origin.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Rao, Aparna. 1992. Ghorbat. In: Encyclopedia of World Cultures, vol. IX: Africa and the Middle East, pp. 105-107. Boston: G.K. Hall. (encyclopedia.com reprint)
sources.note: 'Qazulagi shares its basic structure with Persian; its vocabulary and syntax also contain numerous elements of rural Persian.. a large number of Persian words incomprehensible to the normal Afghan, owing to a manipulation of phonemes, as well as words of Indic, Arabic, and Turkish origin. Some 60 percent of the vocabulary is of an as yet unknown origin.' No phonology beyond this; nothing on stress or tone.
